games.title: Empire
games.note: Walter Bright first designed it as a board game as a child, inspired by Risk, Stratego and the film Battle of Britain.

games.title: Utopia
games.note: Don Daglow's two-player game of rival island nations. Most sources date it to 1981, some to June 1982.

games.title: Hamurabi
games.note: Began as The Sumer Game, Doug Dyment's 1968 adaptation of The Sumerian Game; David Ahl's BASIC version spread it widely.

games.title: Herzog Zwei
games.note: You fly a transforming jet that ferries units into battle. IGN called it arguably the first real-time strategy game.

games.title: Military Madness
games.note: Released in Japan as Nectaris: a turn-based hex war on the Moon.

games.title: Eye of the Beholder
games.note: Westwood's real-time Dungeons & Dragons dungeon crawler.

games.title: Dune II
games.note: Set the template for real-time strategy: harvest a resource, build a base, then produce an army.

games.title: Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun
games.note: Set in a near future where the alien Tiberium crystal is spreading across Earth.

games.title: Total Annihilation
games.note: Chris Taylor's RTS with 3D terrain and units; Cavedog released new units online after launch.

games.title: Supreme Commander
games.note: Chris Taylor's spiritual successor to Total Annihilation; Atari owned that name, so it could not be called a sequel.

games.title: Planetary Annihilation
games.note: Kickstarted in 2012 by Total Annihilation veterans; wars span whole solar systems, and moons can be smashed into planets.

games.title: Age of Empires IV
games.note: Made by Relic, the Company of Heroes studio, returning to Age of Empires II's medieval setting.

games.title: Rise of Nations
games.note: Brian Reynolds, lead designer of Civilization II, put national borders and eight historical ages into a real-time game.

games.title: Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak
games.note: A desert-bound prequel to Homeworld from a studio co-founded by the original's art director, Rob Cunningham.

games.title: Ground Control
games.note: Massive's debut, made in Malmö, dropped base building: squads arrive by dropship and fight over 3D terrain.

games.title: World in Conflict
games.note: A Cold War that turns hot; no base building, players spend points on reinforcements and air strikes.

games.title: Warhammer 40,000
games.note: Rick Priestley's science-fiction miniatures wargame, first published as Rogue Trader.

games.title: Warhammer Fantasy Battle
games.note: Games Workshop's fantasy miniatures wargame, played with painted armies of orcs, elves and knights.

games.title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War
games.note: Replaced resource harvesting with capturing strategic points, which pushes players to keep attacking.

games.title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II
games.note: Dropped base building for a few elite squads that gain experience and gear between missions.

games.title: Company of Heroes
games.note: World War II RTS with destructible buildings, infantry cover and control points instead of resource gathering.

games.title: They Are Billions
games.note: Steampunk colony builder where one gap in the walls can let a zombie horde in. Early access from 2017.

games.title: Stormgate
games.note: Free-to-play RTS from a studio founded by former StarCraft II and Warcraft III developers.

links.took: Real-time control of units and bases on one battlefield, against a live opponent.
links.added: Mouse-driven control, resource harvesting and a sci-fi war over the spice of Arrakis.

src.t: Joe Bostic (Westwood), The Making of Dune II, ReadOnlyMemory

links.extra: Bostic said the team liked elements of Herzog Zwei; producer Brett Sperry stressed it was not the only influence.

links.took: A god's-eye view of a living map that you shape with clicks rather than direct control.
links.added: Turned the overhead view into a war of bases, harvesters and tanks.

src.t: Brett Sperry (Westwood), quoted in Wikipedia: Dune II

links.extra: Sperry: 'The inspiration for Dune II was partly from Populous, partly from my work on Eye of the Beholder.'

links.took: Westwood's experience making a fantasy game run in real time instead of turns.
links.added: Applied real-time play to strategy, with a context-sensitive, mouse-driven battlefield.

src.t: Brett Sperry (Westwood), quoted in Wikipedia: Dune II

links.took: Building and moving armies of distinct unit types across a battlefield.
links.added: Removed the turns, so both sides build and fight at the same time.

src.t: Joe Bostic and Mike Legg (Westwood), via Wikipedia: Dune II

links.extra: Cited alongside Civilization and Herzog Zwei.

links.took: Growing an empire's production and technology to unlock stronger units.
links.added: Compressed it into fast, real-time battles over a single resource.

src.t: Joe Bostic and Mike Legg (Westwood), via Wikipedia: Dune II

links.took: Base building, resource gathering and real-time battles; early builds even reused Dune II's art.
links.added: A fantasy world of orcs and humans, two resources and head-to-head multiplayer by modem or network.

src.t: Warcraft Wiki, Patrick Wyatt on the original brief

links.extra: Lead programmer Patrick Wyatt described the goal as a high-fantasy version of Dune II with multiplayer.

links.took: Westwood's own formula: harvesting, a construction sidebar, base building and factions at war.
links.added: Live-action video briefings, a modern war story and two-player battles over modem and network.
links.extra: Same studio and core team.

links.took: The real-time strategy genre that made Chris Taylor leave Electronic Arts to make his own.
links.added: 3D terrain and units, projectile physics and huge armies with queued orders.

src.t: Chris Taylor, via Wikipedia: Dune II

links.took: Fast, base-building real-time war against a computer or human opponent.
links.added: Metal and energy economies, well over a hundred unit types and a commander unit you must protect.

src.t: Chris Taylor, via Wikipedia: Dune II

links.extra: Taylor named both Dune II and Command & Conquer.

links.took: The harvest, build and fight formula that Dune II established.
links.added: Three completely different races, kept in close balance for competitive play.

links.took: Real-time battles over bases against a live opponent.
links.added: Fantasy armies, peasants gathering gold and lumber, and a story campaign.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Herzog Zwei inspired the developers of Warcraft and StarCraft; no Blizzard quote found here.

links.took: Head-to-head real-time war between two bases.
links.added: Three asymmetric races and online play through Battle.net.

links.took: Blizzard's RTS design, and at first its game engine, which led to the 'orcs in space' jibe.
links.added: A rebuilt engine, three asymmetric sci-fi races and story told through in-mission dialogue.

src.t: Game Developer, 'More than Orcs in Space', 2018

links.extra: Development began right after Warcraft II and its expansion.

links.took: Chunky fantasy orcs and armored humans, and the look of a miniature army.
links.added: Turned fantasy armies into a real-time computer strategy game.
links.extra: Bill Roper reportedly called Warhammer a big influence on Warcraft's art; stories that Blizzard wanted the license are disputed.

links.took: Armored space marines, bug-like alien swarms and an ancient psychic race.
links.added: Blizzard's own factions, balanced for real-time competitive play.
links.extra: A popular fan claim; no Blizzard statement or other solid evidence of direct borrowing has been found.

links.took: GDI against Nod, Tiberium harvesting and video briefings.
links.added: A darker near future, walking mechs, day-night lighting and terrain you can destroy.

links.took: The Tiberium story of GDI and Nod.
links.added: A third faction of aliens, the Scrin, and 3D graphics.

links.took: The real-time strategy boom that made Creative Assembly plan its own RTS.
links.added: Real-time battles with thousands of soldiers inside a turn-based campaign across feudal Japan.
links.extra: Creative Assembly first planned a B-title RTS after Command & Conquer's success.

links.took: History as a strategy game: advancing a civilization through ages with an economy and technology.
links.added: All of it in real time, with villagers gathering four resources and armies from the Stone Age on.

src.t: Rick Goodman (Ensemble), excerpt from Gamers at Work, Game Developer

links.extra: Co-designer Bruce Shelley had helped Sid Meier design Civilization.

links.took: Real-time base building, worker economies and upgrading the town center to unlock buildings.
links.added: Real history, twelve civilizations and advancing through ages.

src.t: Shacknews, oral history of Age of Empires
Flash of Steel, Age of Empires (1997)

links.took: Fast real-time strategy, which Bruce Shelley said is where Age of Empires began.
links.added: Civilization-style history and economics in place of modern warfare.

src.t: Bruce Shelley, GCDC 2007 retrospective, Game Developer

links.extra: Shelley named Warcraft and Command & Conquer as the spark.

links.took: The medieval setting, villagers, four ages and civilizations with unique units.
links.added: Civilizations that play very differently, infantry who build siege engines in the field, and documentary-style campaigns.

links.took: Relic's experience with readable real-time battles and its studio team.
links.added: A classic villager-and-age RTS in the Age of Empires mold.
links.extra: Same studio, Relic Entertainment.

links.took: Brian Reynolds's Civilization design: borders, eras, wonders and city growth.
links.added: All of it in real time, with territory that expands from cities and supply lines for armies.
links.extra: Reynolds was lead designer of Civilization II before founding Big Huge Games.

links.took: The historical real-time strategy formula Age of Empires II popularized.
links.added: Eight ages from ancient to information era and a turn-based-style world conquest mode.

links.took: Chris Taylor's huge-scale RTS: a commander unit, queued orders and two resources.
links.added: Strategic zoom from the whole map down to one unit, and experimental super-units.
links.extra: Same designer; Atari owned the Total Annihilation name.

links.took: Giant-scale wars led by a single commander unit.
links.added: Battles across spherical planets in a solar system, with moons used as weapons.
links.extra: Made by Uber Entertainment, which included Total Annihilation veterans.

links.took: Homeworld's carrier-led fleet and the Kushan people's backstory.
links.added: Moved the war to the desert surface of the planet Kharak.
links.extra: Blackbird Interactive was co-founded by Homeworld's art director Rob Cunningham.

links.took: Fully 3D fleet battles in space with persistent ships between missions.
links.added: Huge space structures to use as cover, and a co-op roguelike mode.

links.took: Massive's RTS without base building, built on squads and reinforcements.
links.added: A Cold War invasion of the United States, drop-in online battles and tactical nukes.
links.extra: Same studio, Massive Entertainment in Malmö.

links.took: The setting, factions and miniatures of Games Workshop's tabletop game.
links.added: Real-time battles with squads, morale and capture points.
links.extra: An official adaptation.

links.took: Relic's squad-based units and strategic points in place of harvesting.
links.added: World War II setting, infantry cover and buildings that crumble under fire.
links.extra: Same studio; both replaced resource gathering with control points.

links.took: The Warhammer 40,000 factions and squad-based combat.
links.added: No base building; a few hero squads level up and collect wargear across a campaign.

src.t: Wikipedia: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II

links.took: Lessons in real-time strategy design that StarCraft II's lead studied while building the sequel.
links.added: Classic StarCraft base-building and three-race balance, with a choice-driven campaign.

links.took: The control scheme; the director calls StarCraft 'the reference' for it.
links.added: A colony that must survive waves of tens of thousands of zombies, with pause-and-plan play.

links.took: Fast competitive RTS design from the people who led StarCraft II.
links.added: Free-to-play, co-op modes and its own demons-versus-humans setting.
links.extra: Frost Giant was founded by former Blizzard RTS developers.

links.took: Running a nation's farms, housing, schools and military to keep its people happy.
links.added: A whole world, rival leaders, a tech tree and history from ancient times to space flight.
links.extra: GameSpot called Utopia 'Civilization 0.5' and said it laid the foundation for Civilization and SimCity.

links.took: Building a settlement you watch and manage rather than a character you control.
links.added: A whole city of zones, traffic, power and budgets with no win condition.
links.extra: No evidence Will Wright played Utopia; the credit comes from critics.

links.took: Exploring a hidden map, founding cities that build units and conquering the world.
links.added: Economics, science, diplomacy and thousands of years of history.
links.extra: Sid Meier has said Empire influenced Civilization more than the board game did.

links.took: Managing scarce food and land each turn as an economy.
links.added: Four players competing on an alien world, with real-time land auctions and action.
links.extra: Byte called M.U.L.E. a cross between Hammurabi, Diplomacy and an arcade game.
